name: Shot glass lip challenge

lead: The shot glass lip challenge involves creating suction over the lips with a small glass so they swell and look fuller for a short while. It spread as a social-media trend.
No clinical research has tested it. Medical sources describe suction plumping as causing temporary swelling.

paras: Suction draws blood into the lip tissue, producing short-lived swelling rather than any lasting change to lip structure.
Bruising and swelling are the commonly reported effects of lip suction and lip procedures generally. There is no regulatory or clinical guidance specific to the trend.

lead: The shot glass lip challenge is a social-media trend in which people press the rim of a small glass or similar container over their mouth and create suction, so that the lips swell temporarily and look fuller. It is a do-it-yourself variant of suction lip plumping, which medical references describe as drawing blood into the lips by vacuum pressure and producing short-lived swelling.[1]

Clinical references on lip augmentation note that bruising and swelling are common after lip procedures and can last from several days to a week, and list irritation, bleeding and uneven lips among possible effects.[1] No published clinical studies have examined the shot glass challenge itself. Sources available for this entry are limited, so this article is short.
infobox: Suction applied with a glass or cup

paras: Participants hold a glass or comparable container against the mouth and draw air out so that suction pulls the lips into it, then share before-and-after images or videos. The effect they seek is temporary fullness, similar to what commercial suction lip pumps are marketed to produce.[1]

Suction pumps work by drawing blood into the lips; medical sources describe the resulting swelling as temporary.[1] News and social-media coverage of the trend has focused on bruising and swelling after attempts; this article does not cite individual reports.
No studies found. Research on lip augmentation more broadly concerns fillers, fat transfer and implants rather than home suction.[1]
